Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:115: Behold, he said, "and then the Holy One, blessed be He, is found full of blessings every day" — and this is the matter of Birkat HaMazon, that it causes the flow of blessings to the Shechinah. And incidentally, the merit is explained of one who asks for his sustenance every day, who is called a son — and it is the way of a son to love his father, and this love is that he causes the flow of blessings above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:116: And further he explains below that regarding those who ask for their sustenance from the Holy One, blessed be He, every day, it is said (Psalms 147:11), "The LORD favors those who fear Him, those who wait for His kindness." And they said in brief: who are His fearers, from whom this favor issues? He then says, "those who wait for His kindness" — those who watch and wait every single day to ask their sustenance from the Holy One, blessed be He — as indicated by the verse "those who wait for His kindness." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:117: Further, in the Zohar (portion Miketz, 199b): he opened and said the verse following it (Proverbs 28:20), "A faithful man will abound with blessings" — this refers to one in whom the Holy One, blessed be He, has faith, such as Rabbi Yesa the Elder, who, even though he had food to eat that day, would not prepare it until he asked for his sustenance before the Holy King; after he prayed his prayer and asked for his sustenance before the King, then he would prepare it, and he would always say, "we shall not prepare until it is given from the King's house." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:118: Some err and say that the blessing "Barech Aleinu" [in the Amidah] constitutes the general request for sustenance, but from this statement there is proof against this, for it says "after he prayed his prayer and [then] asked for his sustenance" — it appears that the matter of prayer is one matter in itself, and the asking for sustenance is a separate matter in itself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:119: And similarly they said in Midrash Tanchuma (Beshalach 20), and likewise in the Mechilta, on the verse (Exodus 16:4), "Behold, I will rain down for you" etc., "a portion for each day" — they said, whoever created the day created its livelihood. From here Rabbi Eliezer of Modi'im would say: whoever has what to eat today and says, "what will I eat tomorrow?" is one of those lacking in faith. Thus far his words. And so they said in tractate Sotah (48b): "it has ceased" — this refers to the people of faith having ceased. Rabbi Yitzchak said: these are people who believe in the Holy One, blessed be He. It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says, whoever has bread in his basket and says, "what will I eat tomorrow?" is only among the lesser in faith. And this is what Rabbi Elazar said: what is the meaning of what is written (Zechariah 4:10), "for who has despised the day of small things"? What caused the table of the righteous to be diminished in the future to come? The smallness of faith that was in them, that they did not believe in the Holy One, blessed be He. Thus far his words. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained that they believe in the Holy One, blessed be He, enough to forgo their money for the beautification of a mitzvah, for charity, and for the expenses of Sabbaths and festivals — [and yet] their table will be diminished in the future to come, meaning they do not receive full reward; and this is the meaning of "for who has despised the day" that comes upon the righteous — the smallness of the small in faith. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:120: And just as a person should not eat until he has prayed for his sustenance, so he should not eat until he has occupied himself with Torah and studied the fixed hour of his study. And so our Sages of blessed memory explained in Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah, portion Nazir, on the verse (Ecclesiastes 10:17), "Fortunate are you, O land, whose king is a free man" — explaining this of one who occupies himself with Torah, who is called free, for Torah is called freedom. And it then says, "and your princes eat in the proper time" — meaning that they fix times for Torah and afterward eat, fulfilling what is said (ibid. 9:7), "go, eat your bread in joy and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds" — this is what is written after it (ibid. 10:17), "in strength and not in drunkenness" — in the strength of Torah and not in the drunkenness of wine. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:121: Although we have explained the intent of eating in general terms, it remains to explain it in particular, for we are obligated to unify [the divine Names] above in all things, as in "let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven" (Avot 2:12), and likewise "in all your ways know Him" (Proverbs 3:6), as explained in the Gate of Love. This was the greatness of the Patriarchs, that even in physical deeds they performed unifications, and the proof is the matter of the wells of water that Abraham and Isaac dug, which is explained in the Zohar (portion Toldot, 141a) as being comparable in significance to our mitzvah of tefillin; see there. And likewise Jacob, in the matter of the rods that he peeled at the watering troughs, which is explained in the Zohar (portion Vayetze, 162a, Sitrei Torah) as intending the laying of tefillin — these are his words: Jacob the perfect one took those rods — tefillin of the head — at the watering troughs, meaning [he made] space and place for the tefillin. Thus far his words. Likewise in the details of eating there is complete unification, as we shall explain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:122: Rabbeinu Bachya, of blessed memory, wrote in the book Shulchan shel Arba (second gate) a fitting matter regarding unification in eating. These are his words: you already know that the existence of the soul is not through the eating of the body, and its actions are not manifest except through the body. From this you will understand the matter of the sacrifices, which is among the secrets of Torah, of which it is written (Numbers 28:2), "a pleasing aroma to My fires [ishai]." Does the power of the supernal soul increase and add through their eating of the sacrifices? So too our Sages of blessed memory said: "My offering, My bread for My fires" — one might think, [it is given] for My bread [i.e., for God's own benefit]; the verse teaches, "to My fires" — you give it to My fires [the fire-offering angels/attendants], and this is because of the binding of the soul: within the attributes, the powers of the soul are bound with the powers of the body. And understand the verse that the sweet singer of Israel mentioned (Psalms 103:1), "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, His holy Name" — he unified the hidden [soul] with the Hidden [God] and the revealed [body] with the Revealed. And this acquisition is that the powers of the soul do not become manifest and do not come to action except through the body; thus the body is a great necessity for publicizing the greatness of the soul and its perfection. And you must know that a person's eating is only illusion — it is not a true thing nor a certain act, for it is a false and changing matter, passing through the intermediate limbs from one cause to another; but the pure thoughts in wisdom, and the attachment of thought to the light of the intellect in the wisdom of Chochmah, is the true and certain eating — as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Vayikra Rabbah 20:6) on "and they beheld God, and they ate and drank" (Exodus 24:11): Rabbi Yochanan said, this is certain eating, as it is said (Proverbs 16:15), "In the light of the king's face is life."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:123: And he said further below: therefore, when he eats, he must free his mind and let it wander toward the Holy One, blessed be He, with every single mouthful, as in what is written, "and they beheld God, and they ate and drank." This is comparable to what our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Bereshit Rabbah 14:9), "Let every soul [neshamah] praise the LORD" (Psalms 150:6) — with every single breath [neshimah], give Him praise. And you can learn this from the generation of the wilderness, for while they ate the manna their intent wandered toward the Shechinah and they intended humility, for this is why wisdom obligated that the measure of their sustenance be an omer, which is a tenth of an ephah — that is, one part in ten of the ephah, corresponding to the reason for the mitzvah of the tithe. For when a person measures nine measures and separates the tenth, the wise contemplate the tenth, which is the attribute that provides prey for its household and provides sustenance for every creature above and below. For this reason they said (Berachot 47b), "nine and a minor combine" — meaning they combine in the blessing over food to bless "let us bless our God," who is the Master who provides sustenance to every creature.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:124: And he said further below: you thus learn that when a person stands at his table and eats with this intent in mind, that eating, though it is a physical matter and a natural act, returns as an elevated intellectual service — this is the reason for what is written (Proverbs 3:6), "in all your ways know Him," as I have mentioned; and if so, his eating is considered a complete service, like one of the divine services or like one of the commandments. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose. We have abbreviated his words to what is needed for our intent, and omitted what is not essential.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:125: What appears to us, as included in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar and in the Ra'aya Meheimna, is that one must intend that the sustenance flows from the right side to the attribute of Tzadik [the righteous, i.e., Yesod], and the Tzadik bestows it to Tzedek [Malchut] — sustenance from the right side. So it is explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, end of 168) regarding "upon the land" and "upon the sustenance": these are his words: "upon the land" — this is the land of the living; "and upon the sustenance" — this is Chesed; behold, this is included in that in a single attachment. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:126: And there (portion Vayechi, 240a), regarding (Judges 14:14), "out of the eater came forth food" — explained that from the Tzadik, who is called "eater," food issues to the lower attribute, which is the Shechinah. These are his words: he opened and said, "out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness" — this verse has support for us. "Out of the eater" — this is the Tzadik, as it is written (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous [tzadik] eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — the Tzadik certainly eats and takes everything; why? "to the satisfaction of his soul" — to give satisfaction to that which is called his "soul," which is called David. "Came forth food" — for were it not for that Tzadik, sustenance would never issue and the world could not exist through it. Thus far his words. It seems to me that "maakhal" [food] equals 91 in gematria, corresponding to the two Names united within the Tzadik, and likewise the sustenance is drawn from the secret of unification, as is explained in the Zohar (portion Vayechi, 240a) on the verse (Psalms 104:15), "and bread that sustains man's heart" — that the word "v'lechem" corresponds to the letters vav-heh; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:127: Further, there (Zohar, portion Vayikra, 11b), regarding the explanation of the Name Shaddai within Tzadik — explained that He is called Shaddai because He says to the world "enough" [dai], giving sufficient sustenance to the worlds. These are his words: the ninth [sefirah, i.e., Yesod] is Shaddai, for it says to the world "enough" [dai], since it is sufficient provision, and provision does not come to the world except from the Tzadik, who is the foundation [Yesod] of the world, who says to the world "enough." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:128: If so, one must intend that just as the supernal attribute of Tzadik eats in order to give satisfaction to his supernal soul, the soul of David, so too he draws the flow from Tzadik, from the right side, and from the attribute of Tzedek, to give existence to his lower soul, which is a portion of the Shechinah. This is along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar, portion Vayera (100b), on "who has not lifted up his soul in vain" (Psalms 24:4) — "my soul" is written [not just "his soul"] — and we have copied his words in the Gate of Love (ch. 11).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:129: And by this we understand what Hillel, peace be upon him, used to say to his students: "come and let us do a kindness with the guest" — and he said that this refers to the poor soul, and we have copied this in the Gate of Love (ch. 11). This is because the flow of sustenance is from the side of Chesed, and therefore it is called "gemilut chasadim" [acts of loving-kindness].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:130: Now, the soul dwells in the heart, as explained in Tikkunim (49a), which we have copied above in chapter 1. We find that the soul, in this aspect of it that dwells in the heart, which is fire, has a judgment quality; therefore one must draw sustenance to it from the right side and quiet its judgments — for on a fast day, when there is no food, a person's fat is melted by the heat of the heart. Afterward he must remember to give it food to eat, for the fire that rests upon his head, the secret of (Deuteronomy 4:24), "for the LORD your God is a consuming fire" — and what is its eating? Torah and the commandments; and this is (Ecclesiastes 9:8), "and let oil not be lacking on your head," as explained above in the Gate of Love (ch. 4). Therefore he should occupy himself with Torah before Birkat HaMazon, as explained, and Birkat HaMazon is a positive commandment, and through this the supernal fire eats — this is why they were strict in portion Vayakhel (218a-b) regarding Birkat HaMazon, since it is a correction for the Shechinah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:131: Further, he should intend what is explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (236a), that Netzach and Hod are called "molars" [tochanot] from the right side, and are called two vavs of the esophagus [veshet] from the left side. These are his words: Netzach and Hod are two halves of a body, like two twins, and therefore they are called "shechakim" [skies/grindings], both together; two vavs — these are from the esophagus, from the side of the left; and they are the two molars of the side of the right. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose. And it is possible that they are called "molars" from the right side because there are 32 paths [teeth] there, and the molars, being part of the 32, refine the waste from the food; see portion Pekudei. And it is possible that they are called the two vavs of the esophagus because the esophagus has two skins, the outer red and the inner white. Now, he should intend that just as above, before the flow reaches Tzadik and Tzedek, it is prepared through the molars and through the esophagus, so he himself grinds through the molars and swallows through the esophagus, to give existence to his soul, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:132: Now, the lower man differs from the supernal man in one respect: for the supernal man, the supernal flow is drawn into him from the brain to the heart and from the heart to the liver, as explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 153a); but the lower man needs to purify the food through the stomach, and the food comes to the liver, and the liver divides the sustenance to all the limbs, and offers up the choicest of the blood to the heart, and the choicest of the choicest of all rises to the brain — these being the vapors from the food, which are the fine part. The reason for this is that man, because of his physicality, needs two aspects: first, that the flow come also to his mouth and he grind it until it is refined through all the vessels mentioned, and afterward, from below upward, it rises to the heart and to the brain, as explained. But above it is the opposite, for above in the brain it is very fine, and it must descend from level to level until it thickens and becomes fit for the lower beings to receive it. There is no instance of the sustenance returning from below upward except on a fast day, when the lower man's food has already been digested and the physical blood brought near to the heart; and after it has been digested, the person offers up his fat to the supernal liver, which is the tenth attribute, and from there to the heart, and from there to the brain (Zohar ibid.), and we shall explain their matter regarding fasting.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:133: My teacher, peace be upon him, wrote regarding the mitzvah of "and you shall eat and be satisfied" (Deuteronomy 8:10), that one should intend in the matter of eating the binding of all the holy [attributes] from below upward, in the secret of (Numbers 28:2), "a fire-offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD." And I add, that just as the body is built from four elements, and the food gives strength to the four physical elements, so too, since the soul's foundation is the four letters YHVH, the secret of (Ezekiel 37:9), "from the four winds come, O breath" — as explained in the Zohar (portion Shemot, 13b) — the soul too benefits from that food; and therefore Birkat HaMazon has four blessings, corresponding to the four ruling chariots, as explained in the Zohar and which we have copied above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:134: Further, it is fitting to intend in eating that everything one eats has a holy interior, with husk and straw mixed into it because of the sin of Adam, and through the grinding it is refined, and one's soul benefits from the interior within it, which becomes blood, while the husk and straw within it becomes residue given to the external [forces]; and since it becomes foul-smelling, certainly the good that was within it has been refined out, and what remains is waste to be cast outside. Therefore one who withholds his bodily functions [too long] transgresses (Leviticus 11:43), "do not make your souls detestable," as explained by our Sages of blessed memory (Makkot 16b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:135: Further, when he takes something from the table in his right hand to bless it, he should intend that he raises it up from the world of the Female to the world of the Male. And in drinking water, he should intend to cool the judgment of the heart and the stomach, since water flows from Chesed, and "mayim" [water] equals 90, and with the word itself, 91, corresponding to YAHDONHAI — thus they are a unification of two Names from the side of Chesed. Further, he should intend the four Names AV, SAG, MAH, BAN, which contain nine yods equal to "mayim" — and there is further secret in this. And all the water goes to the lungs, and the secret of the lungs is explained in the Zohar (portion Pinchas, 236a) to be the Seraphim, and the Seraphim are at the Throne, as it is written (Isaiah 6:2), "Seraphim stood above Him, six wings each," and it is explained in Tikkunim (26a) that this is the secret of the Name of 42 letters, there being six letters for each Name, and the Seraphim stand to cool the fire of the heart, which is the Shechinah, which is judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:136: One who conducts himself in his eating in the manner we have written finds himself as though standing before the Holy One, blessed be He, and will not become a glutton at his table, since he stands before the Supernal King and will not come to take his eating lightly; and humility and awe will be drawn upon him, and then his eating is not to fill his desire — for one who eats to fill his desire removes from himself awe and shame and draws upon himself external craving, and then his whole eating is on the side of the evil inclination, to inflame him and cause him to sin. This is not so for one who thinks that he eats before the Holy One, blessed be He, and that there is no partition separating between him and the Holy One, blessed be He — for he stands and blesses "Blessed are You, LORD, our God, King of the universe," speaking directly as one would speak to a companion, and it is fitting to be careful about what comes out of his mouth and not to remove awe from himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:137: It is fitting to think of the great kindness [God] has done him in bestowing that food upon him, for on account of his deeds he was not worthy of the food, since "the soul that sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4); rather, it is His kindness that feeds both the wicked and the good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:138: And when he considers his evil deeds, he will not come to indulge on the six weekdays, as it is said (Job 3:24), "for my sighing comes before my bread" — and these are the words of the Shechinah when she is, as it were, in exile; and on the six weekdays, when she is called poor, he should conduct his eating like a poor man — and this is called (Psalms 146:5), "whose help is the LORD his God" — for it is enough for a servant to be like his master. But on the day of Shabbat he should indulge, for in his indulgence he fulfills the mitzvah of "and you shall call the Sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), and there is no exile on Shabbat; and he should intend that all his delight is drawn above in the secret of "Eden, river, garden," as explained in the Zohar, portion Yitro.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:139: Also, it is fitting to conduct the matter of eating at a particular time, namely the sixth hour, the time of the meal of Torah scholars, as explained by our Sages of blessed memory (Pesachim 12b). The reason for this is that the attribute of the day is a Torah scholar, divided half to Chesed and half to Gevurah, and the portion of Chesed is the first six hours; therefore the Torah scholar, who holds the middle line, holds to the end of Chesed before the side of Gevurah begins, which is what lies between the two. And in the preceding hours he should intend to give sustenance to his soul, as explained above, since it is written (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — after his soul has been satisfied from Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:140: As for the quality of the food, one should conduct oneself according to Torah, which says (Exodus 16:8), "when the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat, and in the morning bread to satisfy" — and Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "meat to eat" and not "to satisfy" — the Torah has taught proper conduct, that one should not eat meat to satiety. And why did He see fit to bring down bread in the morning and meat in the evening? Because they asked for the bread properly, since a person cannot do without bread; but the meat they asked for improperly, since they could have done without meat. This statement is brought in Yoma (75), where it says: from here the Torah taught proper conduct, that a person should eat meat only at night. Thus far his words. And all these matters have allusion and secret, for meat, which is red, alludes to the attribute of judgment, so it is fitting to eat it at night, which is the attribute of judgment; and bread in the morning, which is the attribute of day, mercy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:141: We may say that although it says one should eat meat only at night, this does not mean literally night; rather, the same law applies from the afternoon prayer time onward, which is considered night according to Rabbi Yehuda regarding praying the evening prayer, and the law follows him, for they said in Berachot (27a), "whoever acts according to Mar acts [correctly], and whoever acts according to Mar acts [correctly]" etc. And on this basis the wording of the verse is precise, which says, "between the evenings you shall eat meat," and does not say "at night." And one who does not fast, and whose custom is to rise at midnight to occupy himself with Torah, finds this way fitting, since there is time for the meat to digest, and sleep will not be increased for him when he rises to occupy himself with Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:142: Now that we have explained the essence of the intent of eating and drinking, according to what we have been taught from Heaven and found in books, we shall explain the corrections of the table, which are ten things, as explained in Midrash Ruth (Zohar Chadash, Midrash HaNe'elam), these are his words: in Birkat HaMazon there are known matters. One, the arrangement of the table according to that time, and it is praiseworthy to arrange the table as one sitting to eat before the King, as it is written (Deuteronomy 14:23), "and you shall eat before the LORD your God." Second, washing of the hands — whoever eats without washing his hands is as though he ate impurity. Third, the manner of washing — that he wash the right hand with the left, and use the left to serve the right, and wash to the measure of the joint that the Sages decreed. Fourth, that one must raise his hands after washing at the time he blesses, and join the two arms together at the time of raising his hands. Fifth, that the blessing must be adjacent to the washing. Sixth, to give bread to a poor person. Seventh, to bless the blessing of "who brings forth bread" and be precise in it, and it is forbidden to eat without a blessing. Eighth, one who eats at his table must not be a glutton and gorger, but eat as one eating before the King. Ninth, there must be words of Torah at his table, and one who is alone and has no one with whom to engage in Torah suffices with his blessings. Tenth, the final washing of hands [mayim acharonim] is an obligation, but no blessing was required over it. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose. And some of these corrections are explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna, portion Pinchas (245a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:143: Regarding the arrangement of the table — besides what is explained, that it be as one eating before the King, it is also because of the honor of the bread, which must be treated with honor, as we shall copy his words regarding "HaMotzi." And so they said in the Zohar (portion Pinchas, 244a): the verse "and a tenth of an ephah" — why "a tenth of an ephah"? Rather, the tenth of the ephah corresponds to Keneset Yisrael [the Shechinah], who is the tenth of the levels, and needs to be given between the two arms, and it is the fine flour of the bread and it is the bread; and because it is the bread, it is not commanded regarding the bread of the seven species — wheat, barley, spelt, etc. — [which have] an appointed angel over the world, and no appointed angel was placed over them except the Holy One, blessed be He, alone. Therefore, whoever disgraces bread and throws it on the ground, poverty pursues him, and one appointed angel is assigned to this, and he pursues him to give him poverty, and he will not leave the world until he needs the help of others. Of him it is written (Job 15:23), "he wanders about for bread, saying, where?" — he wanders about, going, moving from place to place, [asking] "for bread, where?" and there is none who looks after him. This is what is written, "where" [ayeh] — where is the one who has compassion on him, that he not be forgotten. Thus far his words. It is thus explicit that one must treat bread with honor because it is watched over by the Shechinah and not by other officers and appointed powers.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:144: Regarding the second [correction], the washing of the hands — it is said in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, 245): these are his words: second, the washing of hands, to the measure the Sages decreed, since there are five knuckles containing 14 joints, and likewise the left hand has 14 joints, together 28 joints, corresponding to the 28 [numerical value of] YHVH, from those 28 letters of the first verse of the account of creation of which it is said (Numbers 14:17), "and now, let the power of the LORD [koach YHVH, numerically 28] be great" — and the ten fingers allude to the ten utterances of the account of creation. Therefore the masters of the Mishnah established: whoever disgraces the washing of hands is uprooted from the world. Why? Because it contains the secret of the ten utterances and the 28 letters by which the world was created. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:145: Regarding the seventh [correction], to bless "HaMotzi" — it is said there in Midrash Ruth, these are his words: for so said Rav Hamnuna the Elder — there are seven lands, and all are inhabited below, and of all of them the Holy One, blessed be He, chose only this earth [tevel], and of all of them, only in this earth were there those seven species; and in all of them the Holy One, blessed be He, gives every grass and every produce of the earth except these seven species of human bread. Therefore one must be precise about it, since bread is entrusted into His hand and not into the hand of another appointed one — He brings it forth and no other. Therefore "HaMotzi" [who brings forth] and not [any other appointed being who] brings forth. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:146: And in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 16) it says that the letter heh of "HaMotzi" refers to the Shechinah, and one must intend to refine it from husk and straw, which are the kelipot — for wheat has husk and straw, which are exempt from tithe, but the wheat itself, after it is refined from them, is obligated in tithe. These are his words, in brief: therefore in "HaMotzi," once the bet [preposition] has done its work, one must be precise with the heh, that it be clean without waste. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:147: Eighth, that one not be a glutton — explained in Midrash Ruth, these are his words: eighth, that one not be a glutton and gorger, but as one eating before the King, for blessing does not dwell in innards that are found gorging in anger, as it is written (Genesis 25:30), "let me gulp down some of that red, red stuff" — indicating gulping. Why? Because the evil serpent dwells in his innards and is never satisfied, and moreover he is called wicked, as it is written (Proverbs 13:25), "but the belly of the wicked shall lack." Therefore he should conduct himself, when eating, as one sitting before the King. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:148: The remaining corrections of the table were explained above: giving from one's bread to the poor, likewise occupying oneself with words of Torah at the table, and the final washing of hands [mayim acharonim] — these were explained above. And regarding what he said about words of Torah, that if one is alone he is exempt from words of Torah — it appears that the Zohar disagrees with this, in portion Terumah (153b), as we copied his words above, where it says: a table over which no words of Torah were said, it is forbidden to bless over that table — stated without qualification, not distinguishing between a single individual and many. Therefore it is proper to be strict and say some psalm or Mishnah or the like — one who fears Heaven will fulfill his duty for all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:149: And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz wrote, on the Mishnah of three who ate at one table (Avot 3:4), these are his words: and Rashbam, of blessed memory, explained that the verse begins with the altar and ends with the table, to say that when the Temple stood, a person was atoned through the sacrifices and the song of the Levites; now, in place of the sacrifice, he feeds the poor, and in place of the song, he speaks words of Torah. Some are accustomed to sing hymns or psalms after the meal, and this is a good custom to be spared punishment, but the essential thing is really to say some halakhic point, or a novel interpretation of a verse or an aggadah, for there are three categories: the completely righteous, [who do] what we have said; the intermediate, the psalm; the wicked, nothing at all. And just as one who does not speak words of Torah draws upon himself the power of impurity, so one who speaks words of Torah draws upon himself the power of purity, as it is written (Ezekiel 41:22), "and he spoke to me, this is the table."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:150: And he further wrote below: the time of eating tests and refines, to know whether one loves Torah or not — a parable of a man who has a son overseas, whom he remembers at his time of joy; the verse says (Psalms 137:6), "if I do not raise up Jerusalem above my highest joy." Therefore at the time of eating, when a person is joyful, if he remembers Torah, it appears that his love for it is bound in his heart; but when he forgets it amid the food, then the evil inclination becomes inflamed and strengthens its position, and the intellect stumbles and falls — like a parable of two combatants, one falls and the other rises, and from then he has no recovery. Therefore the glory and beauty of Torah are withheld from him from then on, and the time of the meal is a dangerous passage — for if he is then drawn after the evil inclination and Amalek prevails, [it is like] when he raised his hand in the Torah of Moses and Israel prevailed. Thus far his words. It appears from his words, and so I have seen written, that even while he is chewing the food he must contemplate words of Torah, besides the words of Torah at the table, and it is fitting to be strict in this regard.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:151: Regarding the corrections of the table, they elaborated at length there in the Ra'aya Meheimna (245-246), and we have not copied his words in full so as not to be lengthy. They also explained there the corrections of the cup. And in portion Ekev (272b) the corrections of the table for Friday night are explained; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:152: Regarding Birkat HaMazon, it is fitting to think, when he blesses, that he fulfills thereby a positive commandment, and therefore he must not bless it lightly or while dozing off, without intent; rather he should prepare himself to meet his God and bless with his head covered — for us, this covering is that he bless while wearing the head-covering with which he customarily goes out to the marketplace before people. And he should bless with awe and love, as with all commandments requiring awe and love — awe being explained in its place as fearing his Master, who is great and rules, etc. (11b), and love being that he remember the great kindness God has done him, and that He has favored him by preparing his sustenance, even though he was not worthy of it because of his sins — and this is what is meant by "who feeds the whole world with His goodness, with grace, with kindness, and with mercy" etc. — meaning, through His kindness He feeds all, both the wicked and the good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:153: He should take to heart the secret of "Ishmael My son, bless Me" (Berachot 7a) — for although He, blessed and exalted be He, does not need us, since He created the heavens and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that is in it, and all need Him while He needs none of them — nevertheless He desired that He be blessed through the lower beings, so that they be readied to receive of His goodness. Therefore it is fitting for us, His children, to do our Father's will, to bless Him with desire and love, and to bless word by word calmly and deliberately, giving Him praise, as in "and You gave our fathers a desirable land, covenant, and Torah" etc. And he should bless in a loud voice — meaning that his household should hear his voice, that he not bless in a whisper — for saying the blessings aloud arouses the intent and brings remembrance, whether on Rosh Chodesh he remembers "Ya'aleh V'yavo," or on Shabbat "Retzeh" and the like; and one who says it in a whisper forgets everything, along the lines of what our Sages of blessed memory said regarding the occupation with Torah — that it must be brought forth by mouth, as it is said (Proverbs 4:22), "for they are life to those who find them," and likewise "ordered in all things and secured" (2 Samuel 23:5), as they expounded in Eruvin (54a); and so too regarding the blessings.
